extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, mathematicians, and scientists interested in the foundations of mathematics and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Critical examination of the epistemic status of axioms, definitions, and mathematical/deductive reasoning — arguing that these are, in large part, inductions from experience and that deductive sciences are hypothetical. Discusses psychological causes (habit, association) that make empirical truths appear necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as inductions from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Axioms are but a class, the most universal class, of inductions from experience; the simplest and easiest cases of generalization from the facts furnished to us by our senses or by our internal consciousness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat axioms as experimentally grounded generalizations. The burden of proof is on those who claim axioms have a non-experimental (a priori) origin. One should demand positive argument before accepting any claim that axioms are independent of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are generalized fictions, not exact truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in demonstrative sciences are generalizations from experience which are not, accurately speaking, truths; they assert some properties while denying others that in fact accompany and modify them — the denial being a fiction made to exclude modifying circumstances for convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or forming definitions, recognize they are pragmatic simplifications to isolate properties of interest. Evaluate whether excluded modifying circumstances materially affect conclusions before treating definitions as exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive (demonstrative) sciences are inductive and hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive or Demonstrative Sciences are all, without exception, Inductive Sciences; their evidence is that of experience. They are also Hypothetical Sciences: their conclusions are only true on certain suppositions (approximations to truth) and must be tested for applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret proofs as conditional: they show what follows if assumptions hold. Separate (a) derivation of consequences from assumptions (demonstrative work) from (b) empirical inquiry whether assumptions are true or close enough in particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivableness is contingent, not proof of impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Inconceivableness is an accidental thing, not inherent in the phenomenon itself, but dependent on the mental history of the person who tries to conceive it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept 'I cannot conceive the contrary' as evidence that the contrary is impossible. Historical and psychological factors (habit, education, association) can make formerly conceivable states of affairs seem inconceivable; conceptual difficulty does not equal metaphysical impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit and association make empirical truths seem necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated successful application and mental association of ideas can lead scientists to believe certain experimentally discovered laws are of 'demonstrable necessity' and self-evident, although this feeling is produced by habit and familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the psychological effect whereby familiarity with a theory causes its propositions to appear self-evident. Evaluate claims of necessity by tracing their empirical origins rather than by intuition of self-evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses are chosen to group known facts and then tested experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis chosen will naturally be one which groups together some considerable number of facts already known. Men assumed its truth hypothetically, and proceeded to try whether, on more careful examination, the phenomena which apparently pointed to a different conclusion would not be found to be consistent with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing hypotheses, prefer those that account for many known facts. Use experiment to test whether apparent contradictions are resolvable under the hypothesis rather than taking the hypothesis as self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic and algebra are not merely verbal manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that reasoning in arithmetic/algebra is a mere transformation of language is inadequate; there is in every step of an arithmetical or algebraical calculation a real induction — inferences of facts from facts — disguised by extreme generality of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat symbolic manipulations as representing genuine inferences about quantities/things, not as empty definitional slips. Assess whether the implicit generalizations invoked by symbols are justified by experience or appropriate abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers must be numbers of something (no pure abstract numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: “All numbers must be numbers of something: there are no such things as numbers in the abstract.” Propositions concerning numbers are propositions concerning all objects whatever; arithmetic truths are grounded in our experience of collections and separations of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying numerical reasoning, be explicit about what the units/numbers refer to. Use sensory or empirical grounding (counts, partitions) in pedagogy and justification of number statements rather than appealing to abstract self-evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty is limited to pure number and to certainty of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty ... is not an attribute of all mathematical truths, but of those only which relate to pure Number, as distinguished from Quantity in the more enlarged sense; the certainty ascribed to geometry/mechanics is certainty of inference, not guarantee that the suppositions are exactly true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish two senses of certainty: (a) certainty that conclusions follow from premises (logical/demonstrative certainty), and (b) certainty that the premises accurately describe the world. Only the former is generally guaranteed; the latter requires empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic axioms are inductive generalizations (sums/differences of equals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inductions of arithmetic include such principles as: 'The sums of equals are equal' and 'The differences of equals are equal.' These two are sufficient (unequals handled by reductio), and are results of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regard these axioms as empirically grounded generalizations that work because they reflect observed regularities in collections of objects; in application, verify that their underlying conditions hold (e.g., same units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic conclusions presuppose equality of units (the 1=1 condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one hypothetical element in the ratiocination: in all propositions concerning numbers a condition is implied — that 1=1; that all the numbers are numbers of the same or of equal units. Let this be doubtful, and not one of the propositions of arithmetic will hold true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check the uniformity/compatibility of units before applying arithmetic conclusions to quantities. When inferring from number to other attributes (weight, power), the assumption that units are equivalent is empirical and may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative science prepares inferences from assumptions for future use
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative Science investigates what else may be concluded if we find, and in proportion as we find, the assumptions to be true — performing once for all the tracing of consequences of assumptions and keeping results ready to be employed as occasions turn up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstrative reasoning to map consequences of assumptions systematically, but treat the applicability of those consequences to real cases as contingent on empirical validation of the assumptions. Do 'all beforehand that can be so done' and leave observational checks for the particular cases.
